spark.summary: A Data Lakehouse unifies the low-cost, open-format object storage of a Data Lake with the ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and fast SQL performance of a Data Warehouse—typically organized via Medallion (Bronze, Silver, Gold) layers.
spark.keyTakeaway: Store data once in open table formats (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) on cloud object storage, using Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers to progressively refine raw events into governed, query-ready business tables.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional two-tier architectures force teams to pay twice: raw files sit in an ungoverned S3 Data Lake for ML, while curated subsets are copied into an expensive proprietary Data Warehouse for BI—creating data silos, sync lag, and vendor lock-in.
whenToUse: Organizations running both BI SQL analytics and Python/Spark ML workloads over the same multi-terabyte datasets.
When avoiding proprietary storage lock-in (e.g., querying the same S3 data from Snowflake, Trino, Spark, and DuckDB) is a priority.
When teams need ACID mutations (GDPR deletes, CDC upserts, time travel) on cheap object storage.
whenNotToUse: Small datasets (< 1 TB) with purely SQL/BI needs where a managed serverless warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB) requires zero compaction or file-management overhead.
Sub-10ms point-lookup OLTP workloads, which belong in PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, or Redis—not a lakehouse.
Real-time operational alerting requiring < 100ms end-to-end latency, better served by ClickHouse, Apache Pinot, or Flink.
keyPoints: Open table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi) add a metadata transaction log (manifests/JSON commits) on top of Parquet files in S3/GCS/ADLS.
ACID & Time Travel: optimistic concurrency control enables atomic writes, snapshot isolation for readers, and instant rollbacks (`AS OF VERSION` / `TIMESTAMP`).
Medallion Architecture: Bronze (raw, append-only history), Silver (cleansed, deduplicated, conformed entities), Gold (aggregated, business-level star schemas & feature tables).
Compute-storage separation: stateless engines (Trino, Spark, Snowflake, DuckDB) scale independently while reading shared Parquet files via catalog APIs (Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog).
File maintenance is mandatory: background compaction (`OPTIMIZE`), Z-ordering/clustering, and snapshot expiration (`VACUUM`) prevent the small-files problem.

examples.title: Media Streaming Platform Lakehouse Migration
examples.scenario: A video platform stored 400 TB of clickstream logs in S3 Parquet and copied 60 TB into Redshift nightly. Nightly `COPY` jobs took 4.5 hours, and GDPR deletion requests required rewriting entire monthly partitions.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Apache Iceberg on S3 with Spark + Trino eliminated the Redshift copy step, cut storage + compute costs by 42%, and enabled row-level GDPR deletes via Iceberg Merge-on-Read.

examples.title: Logistics Medallion Pipeline for Fleet Telemetry
examples.scenario: IoT GPS pings arrived out-of-order from 80,000 trucks, causing duplicate trip calculations in downstream BI reports.
examples.outcome: The team built a Medallion pipeline on Delta Lake: Bronze ingested raw JSON from Kafka; Silver deduplicated by `(truck_id, event_ts)` via `MERGE INTO`; Gold materialized hourly route-efficiency aggregates for ops dashboards.

tradeOffs.factor: Open Lakehouse vs. Proprietary Cloud Warehouse
tradeOffs.pro: Zero storage lock-in, multi-engine interoperability (Spark, Trino, DuckDB), and 5–10x cheaper raw storage ($23/TB/mo on S3).
tradeOffs.con: Requires managing table maintenance (compaction, vacuuming, manifest rewriting) unless using a managed catalog service.

tradeOffs.pro: CoW delivers fastest read performance because no delete files need to be merged at query time.
tradeOffs.con: CoW rewrites entire 256 MB Parquet files for a single-row update; MoR speeds up CDC writes at the cost of slightly slower reads until compaction.

tradeOffs.pro: Materializing Bronze, Silver, and Gold creates clear replayability, auditability, and decoupled SLAs.
tradeOffs.con: Materializing every intermediate hop triples storage writes and adds end-to-end latency if Silver is needlessly duplicated.

failureModes.name: The Small-Files Problem
failureModes.description: Streaming jobs commit thousands of 50 KB Parquet files per hour, causing query planners to spend minutes listing metadata and exhausting memory.
failureModes.mitigation: Schedule asynchronous bin-packing compaction (`rewrite_data_files`) to target 128–512 MB Parquet files and buffer streaming writes into 1–5 minute micro-batches.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Snapshot & Orphan File Bloat
failureModes.description: Frequent streaming commits accumulate tens of thousands of historical snapshots and unreferenced Parquet files, inflating S3 bills and planning time.
failureModes.mitigation: Run automated snapshot expiration (e.g., retain 7 days) and orphan-file cleanup (`VACUUM`) while preserving tagged compliance snapshots.

failureModes.name: Medallion Layer Leakage
failureModes.description: BI dashboards query Bronze raw JSON directly or Silver tables contain unmodeled business-specific KPIs, breaking clean separation of concerns.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict BI tool service accounts to Gold schemas via catalog RBAC, and enforce Silver-to-Gold modeling in dbt/SQLMesh.

failureModes.name: Concurrent Write Contention
failureModes.description: Multiple Spark jobs or compaction workers update the same partition simultaneously, triggering optimistic concurrency `CommitFailedException` loops.
failureModes.mitigation: Partition writes cleanly by ingestion date/region, use isolated Iceberg branches for backfills, and schedule compaction off-peak or with lock-free MoR.

commonMistakes: Treating Bronze, Silver, and Gold as rigid physical folders that must always be 3 separate materialized tables even when a simple view suffices.
Partitioning tables on high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_id` or `timestamp_ms`), creating millions of tiny partitions and killing query pruning.
Ignoring Parquet row-group sorting (Z-ordering / Hilbert curves) on high-selectivity filter columns like `tenant_id` or `order_id`.
Running `VACUUM` with a 0-hour retention window while long-running queries are still reading older snapshots, causing `FileNotFoundException`.
Leaving raw PII unencrypted or unmasked in Bronze without strict IAM isolation, turning Bronze into a compliance liability.

sections.content:
## The idea

Data platforms evolved across three generations: **Data Warehouses** (schema-on-write, fast SQL, expensive proprietary storage), **Data Lakes** (schema-on-read, cheap object storage, no ACID transactions or schema enforcement—often degrading into data swamps), and **Data Lakehouses**.

A Lakehouse places an **open transactional metadata layer** (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, or Apache Hudi) directly over immutable Parquet/ORC files in cloud object storage. This gives object storage full ACID transactions, snapshot isolation, schema evolution, and partition pruning without copying data into a proprietary warehouse. To keep transformations maintainable, Lakehouses commonly structure data through the **Medallion Architecture** (Bronze -> Silver -> Gold).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a single **Order Event** through a Medallion Lakehouse:

1. **Bronze (Raw Ingestion)**: Debezium streams Postgres `orders` CDC events into Kafka, and Flink appends them as-is into `bronze.orders_raw` (Iceberg) with `_ingested_at` and `_source_offset` metadata. Zero transformations—if a downstream bug is discovered 6 months later, Silver can be replayed from Bronze.
2. **Silver (Conformed & Deduplicated)**: An hourly dbt/Spark job reads incremental Bronze snapshots, deduplicates by `order_id` keeping the latest `op_ts`, casts currencies to `DECIMAL(18,2)`, masks `customer_email`, and `MERGE`s into `silver.orders`.
3. **Gold (Business Aggregates)**: A downstream model joins `silver.orders` with `silver.customers` and `silver.fx_rates` to materialize `gold.daily_revenue_by_region`—a Z-ordered, BI-optimized table powering Looker/Tableau and ML churn features.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / How open table formats achieve ACID on object storage
sections.content:
## How open table formats achieve ACID on object storage

Object stores (S3, GCS) only support immutable object writes, not in-place file updates. Open table formats solve this via **snapshot-based metadata trees**:

- **Apache Iceberg**: Maintains a `metadata.json` pointer (swapped atomically via catalog CAS) -> `manifest list` (per-snapshot partition bounds) -> `manifest files` (per-file min/max column stats) -> `Parquet data files`. Readers prune 99% of files using manifest stats without calling `S3 ListObjects`.
- **Delta Lake**: Uses an ordered `_delta_log/*.json` transaction log plus periodic Parquet checkpoints. Writers use conditional `PutIfAbsent` (or a lock service) to claim the next sequential log version.
- **Hidden Partitioning (Iceberg)**: Decouples physical partitioning (`days(event_ts)`) from logical query filters (`WHERE event_ts >= '2026-11-01'`), preventing user errors that cause full-table scans.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Lakehouse
sections.content:
## Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Lakehouse

| Feature | Data Warehouse (e.g., Redshift, Snowflake) | Classic Data Lake (e.g., S3 + Hive Parquet) | Data Lakehouse (e.g., Iceberg / Delta + Trino / Spark) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Storage Format** | Proprietary internal columnar format | Open Parquet / ORC / JSON | Open Parquet + transactional metadata log |
| **ACID Transactions** | Full ACID | None (eventual consistency, partial writes) | Full ACID with snapshot isolation & time travel |
| **Schema Enforcement** | Strict schema-on-write | Loose schema-on-read (prone to swamp) | Configurable schema enforcement & safe evolution |
| **ML / Unstructured Support** | Limited (requires external export) | Native (Python, PyTorch, Spark) | Native + SQL BI on the exact same copy |
| **Storage Cost** | Higher (bundled or proprietary markup) | Raw cloud object storage (~$23/TB/mo) | Raw cloud object storage (~$23/TB/mo) |
| **Ops Overhead** | Low (fully managed vacuum/clustering) | High (Hive Metastore, manual partitions) | Medium (requires compaction & snapshot expiration) |

## Failure modes

- **Metadata Bottleneck**: Uncompacted Iceberg/Delta tables with 100,000+ small files cause coordinator OOMs during query planning.
- **Over-Partitioning**: Partitioning by `hour` + `country` + `device_type` creates sparse 200 KB files that destroy Parquet compression and I/O throughput.
- **Dangling Delete Files (MoR)**: Heavy CDC `MERGE` workloads using Merge-on-Read accumulate thousands of positional/equality delete files, degrading read latency by 10x until compacted.
- **Catalog Divergence**: Writing directly to S3 Parquet paths bypassing the Iceberg/Unity Catalog causes stale metadata and invisible rows.

## Maintenance and performance tuning

Keep a Lakehouse fast with four automated jobs:

1. **Bin-Packing Compaction**: Merge small files into 256–512 MB Parquet files every few hours for streaming tables.
2. **Data Clustering / Z-Ordering**: Sort rows inside Parquet files by common filter/join keys (`customer_id`, `tenant_id`) so min/max row-group statistics skip 95%+ of blocks.
3. **Snapshot Expiration & Vacuum**: Expire snapshots older than 7 days and delete orphan files > 24 hours old to cap S3 storage growth.
4. **Deletion Vectors / Puffin Stats**: Enable deletion vectors (Delta) or Puffin NDV sketches (Iceberg) to accelerate `MERGE` mutations and join reordering.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Standardize on an open table format (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) backed by a unified catalog (Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog, AWS Glue).
- [ ] Enforce strict separation: Bronze (raw, restricted PII), Silver (deduplicated, conformed), Gold (BI/ML-ready).
- [ ] Target 128–512 MB file sizes and coarse partitioning (e.g., `day` or `month`, never `user_id`).
- [ ] Automate background compaction, Z-ordering, and snapshot expiration jobs.
- [ ] Enable time-travel retention (e.g., 7 days) for instant rollback after bad pipeline deployments.

interviewProblems.title: Architectural Defense: Scaling Data Warehousing, Data Lake & Medallion Architecture
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are leading the design of a distributed application encountering bottlenecks in DevOps & Platform Engineering. How do you leverage Data Warehousing, Data Lake & Medallion Architecture to guarantee high availability?

dimensions.name: Pattern Selection & Execution
dimensions.description: Applying Data Warehousing, Data Lake & Medallion Architecture effectively.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy Data Warehousing, Data Lake & Medallion Architecture with strict monitoring thresholds and graceful degradation fallbacks.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A Data Lakehouse unifies the low-cost, open-format object storage of a Data Lake with the ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and fast SQL performance of a Data Warehouse—typically organized via Medallion (Bronze, Silver, Gold) layers.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Silver Layer applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Gold Layer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Gold Layer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Schedule asynchronous bin-packing compaction (`rewrite_data_files`) to target 128–512 MB Parquet files and buffer streaming writes into 1–5 minute micro-batches.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Store data once in open table formats (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) on cloud object storage, using Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers to progressively refine raw events into governed, query-ready business tables.
Avoid trap: Treating Bronze, Silver, and Gold as rigid physical folders that must always be 3 separate materialized tables even when a simple view suffices.
Avoid trap: Partitioning tables on high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_id` or `timestamp_ms`), creating millions of tiny partitions and killing query pruning.
When to reach for it: Organizations running both BI SQL analytics and Python/Spark ML workloads over the same multi-terabyte datasets.
When to reach for it: When avoiding proprietary storage lock-in (e.g., querying the same S3 data from Snowflake, Trino, Spark, and DuckDB) is a priority.

putItTogether.title: Putting Data Warehousing Lakehouse Together
putItTogether.summary: Store data once in open table formats (Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake) on cloud object storage, using Bronze/Silver/Gold tiers to progressively refine raw events into governed, query-ready business tables.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Data Warehousing Lakehouse before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Migrating to Apache Iceberg on S3 with Spark + Trino eliminated the Redshift copy step, cut storage + compute costs by 42%, and enabled row-level GDPR deletes via Iceberg Merge-on-Read.
